Submit 2026® Cafe Zaffri 2025 New York, NY Food & Beverage Role Interior Design, Branding & Identity Scope Restaurant: Interior Design and Branding Partners Client: Elizabeth Street Hospitality & The Twenty-Two Photographer: Gentl & Hyers Project Narrative The building itself, an idea ahead of it’s time, holds a unique history. Commissioned by heiress Margaret Louisa Vanderbilt in 1891, it was was built for enterprising women, a symbol of agency and voice. Here, a new women-led institution elbows through, and like all true New York establishments, a space that reinvents heritage through irreverent iconoclasm. White tablecloths are an invitation for evidence of enjoyment, celebration, and revelry. Contradiction is at the heart of the Zaf’s concept, one that elevates the exceptional, questions the traditions of hospitality, and provides opportunity for unconventional gatherings and surprising guests. Within the formal and historied architecture of The Twenty-Two, inside a room dripping with luxury lies a story of expression, rebellion, and exuberance. Across interiors and branding , we developed a narrative that balances formality and play. Custom silk wallpaper and tasseled menu books are invitations for long dinners with multiple martinis and fries for the table. Submit 2026® La Playa Hotel 2023 Carmel, CA Hotel, Food & Beverage Role Interior Design Scope Renovation: 67 Room Hotel, F&B Outlets (Bud's), Lobby, Pool, Outdoor Spaces Partners Owner: Marc and Rose Architects: Synectic Design Contractor: Arsenio Branding: Alex Rinker Photography: Chris Mottalini Project Narrative Originally constructed in 1905 by the artist Christian Jorgensen as a gift to his wife Angela, daughter and heiress of the Ghiradelli family fortune. In 1922, the property became a hotel with rooms costing a whopping $2.50 a day. La Playa has continued to evolve alongside the community, "maintaining its eccentric charm and reputation as a haven for writers and artists." Carmel has always been a place of inclusion among California's rock and severe coastal landscape, a place that encourages irreverent thought and exploration. While historic and classic in its architecture and bones, La Playa’s charm and approach is curious and spry. The design of the hotel honors its history and vernacular while ushering in the works and objects of contemporary artists and muses. The resulting effortless eclecticism spans era and trend. Submit 2026® INNESS 2021 Accord, NY Hotel, Food & Beverage Role Building Design, Interior Design, Development Scope New Construction: 40 Room Hotel, Pools, Grounds, Restaurant & Bar, Greenhouse Shop, Outfitter, Gatehouse, Event Barn, Spa & Gym, Golf Course, Tennis Courts Partners Designed in Collaboration: Taavo Somer Development Partners: Taavo Somer, CBSK Ironstate, Lee Pollock Architect: Dutton Architecture Landscape: Miranda Brooks Landscape Design Contractor: RL Baxter Collaborators: Adsum, Beall and Bell, Blended LA, Episode, Holler and Squall, King Collins Golf, Libeco Home, Morentz Gallery, Devon Ojas, Pidjin, Plain English Kitchens, Roll and Hill, Sixpenny, Sonos, WaterWorks, Michael Williams, Works Mfg Photographer: Adrian Gaut Styling: Colin King Project Narrative INNESS is an intimate country refuge and members club located in Accord, New York – about 90 minutes outside New York City. Situated on 225 pastoral acres, its sprawling campus includes 40 hotel rooms (28 cabins, and a 12 room farmhouse), a restaurant and lounge, a 9-hole golf course designed by King Collins, a sports outfitter, swimming pools, tennis courts, hiking trails, an events barn, a farm shop, as well as a 3-acre organic farm embedded into grounds imagined by landscape designer Miranda Brooks. Named after the prominent American landscape painter George Inness, INNESS was conceived by a collaborative team who regularly escaped the city to immerse themselves in the natural spoils of the Hudson Valley. INNESS is a respite from urban living, rooted in the comfort and contentment of the shared experience. A cultural epicenter framed by a stunning landscape. Submit 2026® The LaFayette Hotel and Swim Club 2023 San Diego, CA Hotel, Food & Beverage Role Interior Design Scope Renovation: 139 Room Hotel, F&B Outlets (Quixote, The Gutter, Beginner’s Diner, Le Horse, Lulu’s, The Mississippi Room), Lobby, Cafe, Pool, Outdoor Spaces Partners Owner: Consortium Holdings Architects: Tucker Sadler Contractor: CLTVT, Hawkins Construction, ADK Studios Project Narrative The new LaFayette Hotel & Club brings guests on a creative exploration that features an ode to the original “city within a city” hotel concept moving beyond a one-dimensional space that exudes well curated affluence with aspirational style. Accessible luxury can be found in each of the hotel’s food & beverage vignettes and the 139 rooms featuring custom designed linens and a thoughtfully curated in-room bar amenity featuring a comprehensive spirit and cocktail set-up by venerable cocktail expert Paul McGee. The Lobby Bar iscircular in design under the soaring glass atrium flooding the space with light and is anchored by the Atlas statue and surrounded by a hand-painted ceiling by Brazilian-based artist Joāo Incerti. The bar is constructed with detailed wood surrounded by delicate banquettes with wrought iron lamps and is a convenient meeting space and starting point to the many dining and entertainment rooms held within the hotel. The LaFayette Hotel and Swim Club is home to a range of guest rooms, suites, and townhouses rooted in traditional Victorian, Tudor, and Gothic details. Rich saturations of color, texture, and pattern immerse guests in a fanciful experience that is much more than just a place of rest. Design elements such as wallpaper ceilings, saturated wall tones, fabric draped canopy beds, and burled bar carts read as functional sculpture or art. More results Previous 1 Next Menu Dezeen Close Service Service Magazine Awards Showroom Events Guide School Shows Courses Competitions Topic Topic Architecture Interiors Design Technology Section Section News Features Interviews Opinion Series Videos Talks Podcasts Commercial Commercial Advertise Dezeen Studio Dezeen Dispatch Dezeen Dezeen About Dezeen Contact us Submit a story Cookies policy Privacy notice Subscribe Subscribe Newsletters Follow Instagram Pinterest LinkedIn TikTok Facebook X YouTube Threads Interiors Gjergji Shkurti integrates bar, retail and hi-fi at Million Goods in Brooklyn Ben Dreith US editor 25 September 2026 Share Facebook X Pinterest Reddit LinkedIn Read next London home renovation by Polysmiths uses “light as the primary material” Meta debuts Tamagotchi-style AI agent Splitting cells informs Shanghai research campus’ interconnected buildings Architect Gjergji Shkurti has collaborated with concept shop Million Goods for its second Brooklyn location, using marble, custom millwork and curated furniture to create a transition from hospitality to retail. A glossy red spiral staircase can be spotted through windows that face the buzzy part of DeKalb Street in Fort Greene, Brooklyn. The space became the Million Goods ‘s second shop after co-founder Matt Reyer, who lives nearby, spotting it when it was inhabited by a design studio. Gjergji Shkurti designed the Fort Greene outpost for Million Goods Reyer and fellow co-founder Drew Kaufmann brought on local architect Gjergji Shkurti, founder of Figure Ground , to convert the space. Whereas the original Million Goods in Greenpoint is condensed into a single level, the Fort Greene location gave the team more room to work with, with two levels and an expansive courtyard. The studio revamped a two-level space “I think this was more regal, whereas Greenpoint was a little bit more fun,” Shkurti told Dezeen, referring to the expansive Breccia Pernice stone countertop that forms the wine bar portion on the first level. Stripping the interiors back to their essentials, Shkurti organised the space to provide social areas and retail, integrating them stylistically but separating them physically, with the social spaces on the bottom floor and the retail above. Shkurti designed the space and fabricated the millwork The first-level bar and social space combines multiple different design languages into a contemporary New York style. Behind the bar, metallic speaker boxes were integrated into the custom casework, which was rendered in sapele wood finished in a peca tone. Bridge Street Sound did the sound system, integrating a large speaker directly into the face of the marble bar. Emeco bar stools by Philippe Starck line the bar, and these chairs were used with the wooden banquet seating that hems the space. A backyard takes cues from Brazilian brutalism The ceiling has a distinctly Japanese appearance, with fabric draped between wooden slats. This fabric and an additional layer of insulation were included for sound, but also, with an interesting effect, dampen the lighting from the fixtures above the fabric. A relatively large backyard space was given a central planter for a mature tree. The circular planter doubles as a bench and seating was integrated into the washed concrete walls around the space. Upstairs, a space was included for retail Shkurti said the backyard was designed to evoke Brazilian brutalism. A Louis Poulsen Flindt Plaza post is the centrepiece of the backyard space, rising from the custom pavers. The lighting company sponsored the store and its lamps and fixtures can be found throughout. The refinished facade of the historic low-rise building was refinished with the blessing of the local preservation boards, and the backyard-facing trim was given a red that aligns with the staircase in the front. In the front, the facade was kept black. Read: Safwat by Safwat balances “humor, clarity, and restraint” at Funny Bar in New York The spiral staircase at the front of the shop was original, but given siding and painted a bright red by local fabricator Wood Steel Stone . Wood Steel Stone also completed an impressive central display table on the upper floor that folds aluminium and wood into ply layers with aluminium on top. Upstairs, the original wood from the floors was refinished and used. The team knocked voids in a partition wall to place speakers Shkurti’s custom millwork appears again as casing for the clothing and goods on display, which Reyer described as contemporary and accessible. Through a portal door, a metal stand, also created by Wood Steel Stone was designed to function as both a point-of-sale location and a DJ booth for events. To the sides of the portal door, voids were cleared out to put additional speakers that face into the primary retail space. Above the custom display table is a Louis Poulsen pendant lamp designed to have a vintage look. An upstairs changing area doubles as a point-of-sale station and DJ booth From the upstairs, shoppers can see kids playing basketball on courts across the street, anchoring the location in the neighbourhood. Other recent stand-out interiors include Federico Stevanovich’s studio designed with Nama Studio in Mexico City . Litening bars are increasingly a site of interesting design. Check out seven listening bars from across the globe . The photography is by Joe Thomas . Share Facebook X Pin

More results Previous 1 Next Menu Dezeen Close Service Service Magazine Awards Showroom Events Guide School Shows Courses Competitions Topic Topic Architecture Interiors Design Technology Section Section News Features Interviews Opinion Series Videos Talks Podcasts Commercial Commercial Advertise Dezeen Studio Dezeen Dispatch Dezeen Dezeen About Dezeen Contact us Submit a story Cookies policy Privacy notice Subscribe Subscribe Newsletters Follow Instagram Pinterest LinkedIn TikTok Facebook X YouTube Threads Interiors Wild Form designs with “no straight lines” for bar next to New York’s Stonewall Inn Dan Howarth 27 June 2026 Share Facebook X Pinterest Reddit LinkedIn Read next House of EM draws on mid-century design principles for brick-clad home Eight inspiring homes with bookmaxxed interiors Dezeen In Depth looks at Antoni Gaudí’s impact on global architecture New York-based Wild Form Design Studio has crafted a sculptural interior for a bar called Love Thy Neighbor, which “celebrates the queer community” next to The Stonewall Inn in the West Village . Opened ahead of this weekend’s Pride celebrations in New York, Love Thy Neighbor sits next to the landmark where a series of protests in 1969 became a pivotal moment in mobilising the Gay Rights Movement. The bar features free-form shapes that nod to queerness and individuality Founders Shigefumi Kabashima and Elias Popa, along with Wild Form Design Studio , wanted the bar and dining concept to pay homage to the history of this location, both through design and their approach to hospitality. “Guided by the ethos of no straight lines, Love Thy Neighbor celebrates the queer community, chosen family, and the joys of gathering and belonging,” said the team. Shelves behind the bar follow the “no straight lines” rule set out by the owners Just over the below-grade threshold, a concrete floor panel is gilded with a quote from Marsha P Johnson – a transgender woman who was a key figure in the Stonewall Uprising protests for LGBTQ+ rights, and who continued to fight for queer rights and representation throughout her life. It reads “No pride for some of us without liberation for all of us” in gold letters and includes her signature below. A series of banquettes is divided by sculptural partitions A single brick from the original Stonewall Inn is displayed in a niche at the end of the bar, representing those thrown at the police who raided the bar on 28 June 1969 during the uprisings. “These elements serve as understated reminders of the past, while reinforcing a bright future ahead,” said the team. A single brick from the original Stonewall Inn is displayed in a niche Elsewhere, the curvaceous walls and partitions form an intimate, cavern-like space for 40 guests, and nod to queerness and individuality. “The idea of ‘no straight lines’ became a guiding principle for us,” said Kabashima. “It reflects not only the design of the space, but also how we think about hospitality: fluid, open, and without boundaries.” Spotlights illuminate the bar counter and tables The sculpted surfaces carry warm beige tones across banquettes on the left-hand side, and the bar along the right. A curated selection of liquor bottles and glassware is displayed behind the bar on back-lit shelves, which slant and dip to continue the free-form visual language. The cocktail menu draws on Japanese bartending precision Spotlights illuminate the rounded bar counter and dining tables, directing focus to the food and drinks, while cove lighting traces the fluid edges around the space. In the rear bathroom, a recessed mirror appears to be carved from the thick plaster walls, the vanity has an equally textured edge and features a long, contoured basin, and bronze-hued faucets are suspended from the ceiling. Read: Architecture profession “must engage” in ensuring safety for trans people says Queerscapes founder Love Thy Neighbor’s highly inventive cocktail menu draws on Japanese bartending precision, and uses techniques like clarification, infusion and carbonation to create innovative ingredients like wasabi gin and homemade cola. Drinks are presented in delicate glassware, while Asian-influenced bar snacks and shareable plates are served on hand-crafted ceramics. The rear bathroom features a recessed mirror and a rough-edged vanity “We wanted Love Thy Neighbor to be a space where people from different walks of life can share a delicious meal, connect, and feel like they belong under one roof, at any time of day,” said Papa. “We want guests to feel a sense of freedom here, both in how they experience the space and how they connect with others,” added Kabashima. The basin is contoured and faucets hang from the ceiling Many queer spaces are under threat from a variety of social, urban and economic issues, and continued support is needed to protect venues used by the lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender and queer (LGBTQ+) community. The transgender community is particularly being targeted in the US and UK. The architecture profession “must engage” in ensuring safety for trans people, the founder of Queerscapes told Dezeen in an interview last year. The photography is by Aichan Mama. items.title: Wild Form Design Studio Shapes a Queer Sanctuary in New York | Hospitality Design
items.text: Wild Form Design Studio Shapes a Queer Sanctuary in New York | Hospitality Design Emerald Media Network Advertise Follow Follow Follow Follow Follow Latest View All Posts » News Projects Products Podcast People Resources Topics View All Topics » Hotels + Resorts Food + Beverage Development Interviews Event News Business + People Products View All Products » Roundups Resources View All Resources Webinars Events More About Us Advertise with Us Contact Us Subscribe Latest Topics Products Resources Events More Subscribe View All Posts » News Projects Products Podcast People Resources View All Topics » Hotels + Resorts Food + Beverage Development Interviews Event News Business + People View All Products » Roundups View All Resources Webinars About Us Advertise with Us Contact Us Q MENU Trending Kimpton Miralina Resort & Villas Opens in Scottsdale 2026 HD Awards Winners Five on Friday: October 23rd Most-Anticipated Hotel Debuts Fairmont New Orleans News Wild Form Design Studio Shapes a Queer Sanctuary in New York Love Thy Neighbor unfolds as a sculptural, monochromatic space rooted in community and belonging Published: June 2, 2026 By Stephanie Chen Photos by Alexander Tatsuto Zeren + Aichen Mama New York’s West Village has welcomed Love Thy Neighbor , a 40-seat all-day bar and dining concept that gives new meaning to community through hospitality. Brought to life by bartender and restaurateur Shigefumi Kabashima and chef Elias Popa, the intimate venue takes shape as an atmospheric evening cocktail destination, with daytime service forthcoming. At its core, the space is a celebration of the queer community and the joys of chosen family, anchored by a design ethos that embraces fluidity and rejects rigid boundaries. “The idea of ‘no straight lines’ became a guiding principle for us,” says Kabashima. “It reflects not only the design of the space, but also how we think about hospitality: fluid, open, and without boundaries. We want guests to feel a sense of freedom here, both in how they experience the space and how they connect with others.” A hand-shaped environment Collaborating with Jun Qin of Wild Form Design Studio , the founders stripped down traditional church architecture to create a contemporary environment. Vaulted archways and curved, sculpted booths envelop guests in a comforting embrace, grounded by a warm, monochromatic beige palette inspired by sand and earth. “We wanted the entire space to feel as though it was sculpted rather than conventionally assembled, so many of the walls, seating areas, ceilings, and curved transitions were created through hand-shaped cement work,” explains Qin. “The microcement surface finish helps unify the entire environment visually, while also preserving a soft and natural texture throughout the space.” Rather than relying on one dramatic focal point, the architecture relies on cohesive, custom-designed elements. From the niches to the lighting details, the organic curves create a calming, emotional experience. Details to discover at Love Thy Neighbor Throughout the space are details that honor history and community. A single brick from the original Stonewall Inn is embedded within the bar, while a quote from late activist Marsha P. Johnson, which reads “No Pride For Some of Us Without Liberation For All of Us,” is set into the floor at the entrance. “My goal with the space was to embrace our history, paying respect to the literal bricks laid down by our neighbors like the Stonewall Inn, and to create a space that felt warm, embracing, and inclusive,” notes Popa. “Hence, the highlighted brick in the wall at the end of the bar, pulled from Stonewall. A cheeky homage to our shared history.” He continues: “In design, I love when things are clandestine, objects are hidden and only revealed to those who know where to look. This whole bar is an exercise in restraint and subtlety. At the end of the day, we really wanted to create a space that feels transportive, like as soon as you step into the restaurant you feel like you aren’t in New York anymore—even for just a moment.” Posted In: News ADVERTISEMENT ADVERTISEMENT Related Posts Five on Friday: October 23rd, 2026 Fairmont New Orleans Readies for November Debut Pirajean Lees Brings Mimi Kakushi to Miami Beach Maritime Heritage Shapes Oyster Estate in Greenport General News Projects Products Podcast People Resources Topics Hotels + Resorts Food + Beverage Development Interviews Event News Business + People Resources Webinars Downloads About Us About Us Advertise with Us Contact Us Contact Us Address: 100 Broadway 14th Floor, New York , NY 10005 Social: Follow Follow Follow Follow Follow © 2026 Emerald X, LLC. More results Previous 1 Next Menu Dezeen Close Service Service Magazine Awards Showroom Events Guide School Shows Courses Competitions Topic Topic Architecture Interiors Design Technology Section Section News Features Interviews Opinion Series Videos Talks Podcasts Commercial Commercial Advertise Dezeen Studio Dezeen Dispatch Dezeen Dezeen About Dezeen Contact us Submit a story Cookies policy Privacy notice Subscribe Subscribe Newsletters Follow Instagram Pinterest LinkedIn TikTok Facebook X YouTube Threads Interiors Rockwell Group eschews 90-degree angles for Skywalker Grill at Lucas Museum Dan Howarth 26 September 2026 Share Facebook X Pinterest Reddit LinkedIn Read next Hayhurst and Co carves triple-height void through 1970s Hampstead townhouse Six designs that freshen up the humble toothbrush This week we revealed the Dezeen Awards shortlists Here’s a closer look inside the newly opened Lucas Museum of Narrative Art , where design studio Rockwell Group has outfitted a restaurant and bar that “responds to the museum’s distinctive biomorphic architecture”. Rockwell Group ‘s Los Angeles office designed the Skywalker Grill without a single 90-degree angle, continuing the sweeping curves of the building by MAD Architects . The Skywalker Grill features no 90-degree angles to echo the Lucas Museum’s biomorphic architecture The eatery also references the warm cherry wood interiors of Skywalker Ranch, a 4,700-acre filmmaker’s retreat and workspace owned by Star Wars director George Lucas in Marin County, California. Overlooking the Los Angeles skyline, the fifth-floor restaurant and bar is named after the sci-fi media franchise’s principal character. It is open to both museum visitors and the general public for lunch and dinner. Entry to the fifth-floor space is via a corridor wrapped with cherry wood panels “Responding to the museum’s distinctive biomorphic architecture, the restaurant features no 90-degree angles,” said the Skywalker Grill team. “Curved walls are wrapped in individually crafted cherry wood panels, with no two panels alike, while finger-raked cherrywood columns echo the tambour banquettes lining the perimeter of the room.” Shimmering tiles cover the front of the snaking bar, while the back bar is clad in illuminated Corian Guests arrive via elevator to a corridor that leads to the host stand, lined on one side with cherry panelling that folds up and over the ceiling. Booths are formed with swooping partitions that organically rise and fall in height, and curve to create intimate pockets for conversation. The cherry used throughout the restaurant is a nod to the wood found at George Lucas’s Skywalker Ranch in Marin County A central island is ringed by a green crushed velvet banquette that matches the booth upholstery, and surrounded by circular tables and freestanding dining chairs in soft grey. Tamboured cherry-wrapped columns rise at slight angles and branch like tree trunks to meet the ceiling, which opens in the middle to reveal a beige plaster surface illuminated by cove lighting. A large ovoid window opens onto a terrace with panoramic views The snaking, glossy white bar counter is fronted by shimmering fluted tiles covered in crystal silver leaf, while illuminated Corian forms the back bar. A large ovoid window features operable glass panels that provide access to the outdoor terrace, where further seating enjoys views over the University of Southern California campus towards Downtown LA. Read: MAD’s spaceship-like Lucas Museum revealed ahead of opening “The design incorporates elements of cinematic storytelling, including framing, light, scale and atmosphere, while pairing high-tech materials with handcrafted details,” said the team. The restaurant’s American-style menu features California-grown ingredients, including Wagyu beef and honey ricotta sourced from Skywalker Ranch. Curved, undulating partitions form intimate dining booths Set in a 13-acre landscaped site near Los Angeles’ Exposition Park, the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art is dedicated to storytelling and features a variety of galleries, theatres and educational spaces. MAD and Stantec wrapped the building in over 1,200 curved panels, creating an extraterrestrial form that wouldn’t look out of place in one of Lucas’s beloved movies. The terrace enjoys panoramic views over Los Angeles Rockwell Group is known for its theatrical hospitality projects that immerse diners in atmospheric spaces. Other recent examples include an art deco-influenced Manhattan steakhouse , a revolving restaurant above Times Square and a “cathedral of fried chicken” . The photography is by Tom McGovern . items.title: Skywalker Grill at the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art — Rockwell Group
items.text: Skywalker Grill at the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art — Rockwell Group Skip to content Studio Work Contact News About People Books Careers Skywalker Grill at the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art Announcements 08.11.26 On September 22, 2026, Los Angeles will welcome a new dining destination with the debut of Skywalker Grill, the signature full-service restaurant atop the Lucas Museum of Narrative Art. Designed by Rockwell Group's Los Angeles office and operated by Rhubarb Events & Hospitality Collection, part of Oak View Group (OVG), Skywalker Grill draws inspiration from the welcoming spirit of George Lucas' legendary Skywalker Ranch, pairing classic American cuisine with warm hospitality and sweeping views overlooking Los Angeles. The restaurant blends contemporary and Midcentury Modern influences with sculptural architectural forms to create a dining experience that feels both timeless and inviting. Cherry wood wraps the restaurant's walls and ceiling in individually crafted panels, creating warmth and texture throughout the dining room, while softly illuminated white onyx Corian surfaces introduce a subtle sense of light and movement. At the center of the space, a sculptural bar anchors the restaurant, surrounded by intimate seating areas designed to foster conversation and connection. "The Lucas Museum celebrates the power of storytelling, and we wanted Skywalker Grill to become part of that narrative," says David Rockwell, Founder and President, Rockwell Group. "Our design echoes the museum’s craftsmanship and innovation while introducing moments of intimacy, warmth, and surprise. From the glowing Corian surfaces to the handcrafted cherry wood detailing, every element was designed to create a sense of wonder that feels tactile and welcoming." Read the full press release here . When designing the project, NM3 drew on the influential design of Loos’s famous bar , an early modernist landmark finished in 1908. Photography Previous Next Photography Close “The American Bar was more of an aspiration than a direct formal reference,” studio co-founder Francesco Zorzi told Dezeen. “The ambition was never to recreate Loos’s bar, nor Robert and Trix Haussmann’s Kronenhalle in Zurich, which was another important reference for the project,” he explained. “Rather, we wanted to create a truly classic bar for Milan, with a very specific spatial and architectural character.” Located just across the road from the city’s popular Bar Basso , Bar Bardo is housed within a 55-square-metre single room with an additional bathroom. Almost every element in the listening bar was custom-designed by NM3, known for its modernist-style stainless steel furniture that has already made the young studio a household name in Milan since its founding in 2020. The walls and ceiling were clad with polished rosewood panels, which add character to the small space while improving its acoustics. A quintessentially NM3 stainless steel bar was placed in the centre of the room, where its gleaming surfaces reflect globular 1950s pendant lights by Italian architect Luigi Caccia Dominioni. The lamps are the only vintage pieces in the bar. NM3 swapped their original chains for longer black ones. Photo by T-Space The perimeter of the space features built-in red velvet banquette seating, which matches crimson curtains and a series of bright red speakers fitted across the bar to accommodate a stainless steel DJ booth and metal shelving for vinyl records. Bar Bardo was purposefully designed to be a flexible space. Every interior element is movable, with the exception of the bar and the banquettes. Read: “Progressive spirit” of Space Age interiors informs Barcelona cocktail bar “By simply removing the furniture, the cocktail bar can easily be transformed into a club,” said Zorzi. “The flexibility of the space is therefore achieved through a simple architectural arrangement rather than complex spatial interventions.” At the back of the space, the striking bathroom was covered with bright red 10-centimetre-by-10-centimetre tiles, from floor to ceiling. Photo by T-Space Utilitarian stainless steel was once more selected for the toilets, sink and other fixtures, while pared-back sconce lights illuminate the cubicles. Bar Bardo marks a softer design direction for NM3. The studio previously conceived a “raw” interior for Milan’s Galleria Montegani , as well as a similarly metal-heavy store in the city for fashion brand Miss Sixty. Ahead of Milan design week in April, NM3 was among the studios that spoke to Dezeen about what it’s like to be a contemporary designer in Italy’s design capital. Photographs Previous Next Photographs Close The 307-square-metre restaurant in central Soho sits on a corner and is made from two formerly separate units, which Box 9 combined to make Kid , a modern take on a Turkish mangal restaurant. While the Frith Street side of the restaurant has a more traditional Victorian feel, the Bateman Street side was given a contemporary design, with the use of brick joining the two sites. “The site’s two shopfronts offered an opportunity to connect their contrasting elevations through a shared design approach,” Box 9 co-founder Lou Davies told Dezeen. “Frith Street retains a beautiful Victorian upper storey with distinctive brick patterns that reflect Soho’s merchant-trading history, while Bateman Street has a new elevation and a central section rising to the residences above,” she continued. “The building itself suggested uniting the spaces with a single material.” Brick was chosen not just because of its use in the building the restaurant is located in, but also because of its connection to traditional hospitality spaces and the Turkish heritage of Kid chef Sertaç Dirik. “Brick became central to the concept because it connected so many elements of the project,” Davies explained. “It has a centuries-old relationship with restaurants, kitchens and cooking with fire, forming the basis of traditional fireplaces and hearths,” she continued. “It also reflected the heritage of Turkish cooking and Sertaç’s family background, while connecting to the history of the Soho building and its original brick patterns.” Guests enter the two-storey Kid restaurant through a discreet door on Bateman Street, where they are met by a large, central grill. Like most of the interior at Kid, this was made from material company Kenoteq ’s K-Briq, which is crafted from at least 90 per cent recycled construction and demolition waste and requires no fossil fuels or firing to produce. Read: Gundry & Ducker draws on French dining culture for London restaurant Cassette According to Box 9, this means that it releases a tenth of the carbon emissions of traditional fired-clay bricks. “We loved the idea of using brick on every surface,” Davies said of the material choice. “There was a raw humbleness to it: wine cellars, kitchens and grills would traditionally have been built with brick,” she continued. “It wasn’t about fancy materials; it was about using the best material for the purpose.” Upstairs, visitors will also find the wine room, which seats 14 people and was similarly made entirely of brick. The studio chose slightly different designs to define the two upstairs rooms, using a traditional bond with a traditional joint for the Victorian side and a soldier bond and a raked joint for the more contemporary section. Downstairs, Box 9 designed Kid’s open bakery, which features moveable bespoke tables by design firm Jan Hendzel Studio to allow the room to be used as an events space. Overall, the main aim for Box 9 was to create a space that would complement Dirik’s food, which was formed through his cooking at his family’s restaurant Mangal II. “We needed to create a completely unique restaurant that represented Serta,” Davies concluded. “His personality is big, and his background is rooted in generations of cooking in Turkey and his family’s cooking style, as well as how they cooked at Mangal II. All his training was in cooking with fire.” London has seen a spate of recent restaurant openings, including a French-style restaurant by Cassette and a London pizzeria designed by Isern Serra . The Dean Munich is the latest offering from the Irish hotel chain , with 281 rooms and suites, three bars, and a signature Japanese restaurant named Ibasho. The design blends influences from art nouveau and 1980s nightclubs The project saw von Stein revamp an existing hotel in the city’s Westend neighbourhood, with a design where shades of gold and red extend across velvet furniture, floral carpets, stained-glass windows and ornamental lamps. The project allowed the interior designer to dig into the design history of the city where she was born. Her scheme blends the city’s distinct Jugendstil style, the manifestation of art nouveau in Bavaria, with the decadent nightclubs that proliferated in the 1980s. The lobby features a restored floor of black stone chevron tiles “This is a city rooted in history but always drawn to reinvention,” said von Stein. “I wanted to capture that tension, somewhere between elegance and exuberance, and let it guide every surface, object and gesture.” “The design also brings to life a side of Munich only locals truly know – its rich musical and cultural spirit, quietly woven into the character of the city.” On a raised platform, a wrap-around bar is set below a circular ceiling recess The most radical interventions are in the communal areas on the ground floor, which were completely reorganised. They begin with the lobby, a space with a rich sense of theatricality. At its centre is a stepped platform, where a wrap-around bar is set below a circular ceiling recess with a reflective surface and a decorative wallpaper frieze around its edges. A pair of sphinx table lights were among the vintage pieces sourced for the lobby This is the first of many playful ceilings that feature throughout the hotel. On either side of the bar, lounge areas are framed by tiered ceiling recesses with zigzagging corners, matching the edge details of the internal columns. Read: Traditional wooden townhouses inform interiors of Kengo Kuma-designed Capella Kyoto hotel “We’re really interior architects, so we start with layout and hard finishes before slowly making our way into furniture and fixtures,” von Stein told Dezeen. “I love to fully envelop people in a world, and that starts with the envelope. So ceilings certainly play a big part.” Fluted ceilings and stained glass windows characterise Ibasho’s interior Over the restored chevron-tiled stone flooring, the rest of the space is carefully layered with patterned rugs and gloss-backed sofas, while focal points include bell-shaped sconces, frilled stools and sculptural tables. Many of the objects here were custom-designed by von Stein, although she also sourced some vintage pieces, including original late-19th and early-20th century pieces by Austrian design icons Josef Hoffmann and Otto Wagner. She points to a pair of sphinx table lights as a personal favourite in this room, “somehow out of place, but fabulous”. A conversation pit is set below a gridded mirror ceiling Japanese influences come into play in Ibasho, inspired by the cuisine of chef Alex Craciun. Below mirrored and fluted ceilings, von Stein created a series of “rooms within rooms”. These include a conversation pit with gold velvet sofas and a horseshoe-shaped marble bar encircled by pink leather Verner Panton chairs. Pink leather Verner Panton chairs encircle a horseshoe-shaped bar The Jugendstil-inspired stained glass frames a series of windows between these spaces, offering glimpsed views between them. “For me, the most compelling hospitality spaces are those that reveal themselves gradually,” said von Stein. Noren features a timber-panelled ceiling and tapestry-style upholstery “We wanted to create a space which engages the senses, influences mood and encourages a certain rhythm of experience and connection throughout the diner’s experience.” Tucked away behind Ibasho, Noren is a more exclusive and intimate cocktail bar. This 48-seat space features Friendly Pressure speakers, a geometric timber ceiling and tapestry-style seating. The timber-panelled bedrooms feature a palette of olive greens The style is more pared-back in the bedrooms, but no less stylish. W1T 6AJ T +44(0)20 7436 8846 Hong Kong Ground Floor 12 Kennedy Street Wan Chai Hong Kong T +852 2804 1138 The Magistracy, Hong Kong Set for a dynamic renaissance, we brought back to life Hong Kong’s historic judicial house, The Magistracy, together with hospitality pioneers Black Sheep Restaurants . The Magistracy Dining Room takes its cues from London’s most historic and traditional restaurants. The high vaulted ceilings and carved timber panels reignite memories of the structure’s historical significance, while rich oxblood leather seating and warm golden accent lamps create a plush and generous setting for guests to unwind. Through vast arched detailed glass doors, the Majestic Dining Room spills out onto the Botanical Garden – a lush space abundant with green foliage. A maze of draped ivy, hydrangeas and ferns in terracotta and antiqued planters – the terrace feels immediately reminiscent of British heritage gardens. Hidden away from the busy Hong Kong streets, the Botanical Garden offers a welcome oasis for guests to unwind and enjoy the city’s finest gin & tonics and dishes helmed by MICHELIN-starred Executive Chef Matthew Kirkey. W1T 6AJ T +44(0)20 7436 8846 Hong Kong Ground Floor 12 Kennedy Street Wan Chai Hong Kong T +852 2804 1138 Prince and the Peacock, Hong Kong As the second phase of The Magistracy in Hong Kong, a historic judicial house which has been sensitively reimagined and restored by Black Sheep Hospitality Group in Hong Kong. Featuring a 60-seat main dining space, alongside two unique private dining rooms, and a sports lounge named Jack’s Racquet Room. The spaces are inspired by the rich cultural impact and patronage of the Maharajas, Maharanis, Nawabs, Nizams and Emperors who ruled India’s diverse patchwork of territories before, during and after the colonial era. Just as the country’s aristocrats and monarchs developed intertwined food and artistic cultures, the design of Prince and the Peacock is designed to meld effortlessly with the aromas and flavours of the cuisine created by Chef Palash Mitra of New Punjab Club in Hong Kong, the world’s only Punjabi restaurant with a Michelin star. An invocation of the opulence of historic royal palaces and courts, the peacock takes centre stage in a subtle blend of motifs and vibrant colours inspired by the legendary bird, which still serves as India’s icon of royalty and power. Adjacent to the balcony space hang traditional punkah fans, reminiscent of palatial interiors where the fanning of fresh air was a regal requirement. The Magistracy has been expanded with two private dining room options on the second floor. The first, named the Ruby Room, is designed to host groups of up to 8 people and has been artfully decorated in scarlet tones with a stunning tiled ceiling. The second space, The Kohinoor, was named after one of the world’s largest cut diamonds and holds up to 8 in a room resplendent with elegant pink ceiling drapery. ” This lounge and bar space blends the classic elegance of South Asian sports clubs, with the comfort and sophistication of everything you’d expect from a modern hospitality setting. The space features rich, dark rosewood timber, recalling clubrooms of old, while the lounge area exudes plush comfort with mohair, velvets, and leather armchairs, creating an inviting and luxurious atmosphere. The colour palette is inspired by traditional sports, found in the deep red of cricket balls, warm mustard tones, fresh lime green, and the orange hues of red travertine, as well as striped fabrics drawing on classic club jersey styles.” -Joyce Wang Jack Racquet’s Room blends the classic elegance of South Asian sports clubs with the comfort and sophistication of everything you’d expect from a modern hospitality setting. The space features rich, dark rosewood timber, recalling clubrooms of old, while the lounge area exudes plush comfort with mohair, velvets, and leather armchairs, creating an inviting and luxurious atmosphere. The colour palette is inspired by traditional sports, found in the deep red of cricket balls, warm mustard tones, fresh lime green, and the orange hues of red travertine, as well as striped fabrics drawing on classic club jersey styles. Photos by Oscar Mendoza, courtesy of Josephine The Rundown Los Angeles Josephine Brings Cozy Vibes and French-Italian Cooking to Silver Lake By Kelly Dobkin , an L.A.-based writer and editor. She has contributed to Bon Appétit, Michelin, and the Los Angeles Times, and is a former editor at Thrillist, Zagat, and Eater. She’s also a culinary school grad and recovering waitress. Josephine 4.4 · French-Italian · $ Silver Lake Book Now Published: Oct. 16, 2026 After 20 years cooking in some of the country’s most storied kitchens, there’s something about opening a restaurant with your best childhood friend that just feels like coming home. After opening inside a vintage Craftsman house in Silver Lake earlier this summer, Josephine draws from the personal nostalgia of two California natives, including family recipes reimagined, and nods to their 1990s childhood bedrooms. The buzzy new restaurant looks like equal parts dive bar and rustic Tahoe cabin, but feels like nonna’s house, with hearty slow-cooked dishes and pastas that lean heavily into French and Italian influences. Here are five things you need to know before dining at Josephine. MORE FROM RESY The Rundown Transport Yourself to the South Pacific at Tiki Residency Savage Seas By Esther Tseng The Rundown Brick Lane Brings an Upscale Take on East London Indian Food to the Arts District By Caitlin White The Rundown San Damian Brings Baja California Vibes and Mexican-Inspired Mariscos to Venice By Kelly Dobkin Letter of Recommendation Henrietta Is The Day-to-Night Restaurant Every Neighborhood Deserves By Caitlin White It’s the product of a lifelong friendship. After a shared childhood playing hockey together in San Jose, Anthony Dragotto and Marco Gagliardi worked in very different fields throughout most of their twenties and thirties. Gagliardi sharpened his culinary chops at spots like Zahav , Vetri Cucina, and High Street on Hudson in Philadelphia, as well as Bon Delire in San Francisco, while Dragotto worked in various industries, including tech sales, back in California. It wasn’t until these two old friends reunited at the Oasis concert in Pasadena that they started cooking up the idea for Josephine. “We just kept talking about it, joking about it, drinking over it, and then we decided: ‘All right, screw it, let’s start a restaurant,” Gagliardi says. When it came time to brainstorm, they discovered another connection: both Marco’s great grandmother and Anthony’s grandmother shared the same first name. And just like that, Josephine was born. A summe
